parts.title: Booking a cycle tour
parts.context: A woman phones a company that runs guided cycle tours.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a woman telephoning a company that organises cycle tours. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Good morning, Two Rivers Cycle Tours, Oliver speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Oh, hello. I'm thinking of booking one of your guided bike tours for my family this summer. I saw your advert in a travel magazine, and it looked like a lot of fun.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That's great. I'll just take a few details first, and then I can tell you about the tours that might suit you.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The woman saw the advert in a travel magazine, so 'travel magazine' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Right. Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, it's Helen Thornbury.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: And how do you spell your surname?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: It's T-H-O-R-N-B-U-R-Y.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Thank you, Mrs Thornbury. And how many of you would be coming?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Well, there's my husband and me, and our two children. Oh, wait, I nearly forgot. My nephew is staying with us that week, and he'll definitely want to come. So that's two adults and three children.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That's fine. Children need to be at least eight years old for our tours. Is that OK?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Yes, the youngest is ten, so there's no problem there.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Great. We collect everyone from their accommodation in the morning, so could you tell me where you'll be staying?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: We wanted to stay at the Riverside Inn, but it was fully booked, so we've got rooms at the Kingfisher Hotel, in the centre of town.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Ah, the Kingfisher. I know it well. It's right on our usual route, so that's easy. And which day were you thinking of?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: We arrive on the twelfth of August. We'll be tired after the journey, so not that day. I was going to say the thirteenth, but my husband has an online meeting that morning. So could we make it the fourteenth?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: The fourteenth of August. Yes, we still have places on that day. Now, lunch is included on all our tours. Does anyone in your group have any special dietary needs?

script.speaker: helen
script.text: None of us have any allergies, but my husband doesn't eat meat. He's been vegetarian for years.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That's no problem at all. I'll make a note of that.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: So, there are three tours that are suitable for families. The first one is called the Valley Trail. It's 25 kilometres long, and it's the easiest of the three, because it's almost completely flat.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: Why is it so flat?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Because most of the route follows an old railway line. The trains stopped running about sixty years ago, and the track was turned into a cycle path. Children love it, because you ride through two tunnels.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: That sounds perfect. How much is it?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: It's 45 pounds per person, and that includes bike hire and lunch.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: OK. And the second one?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That's the Castle Circuit. It's a bit longer. The old signs along the route say it's 30 kilometres, but they're wrong, actually. We measured it properly last year, and it's 32.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And what do you see on that one?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: In the morning you stop at Ashby Castle, and after lunch there's a visit to a vineyard, where the adults can taste the local wine. The children get grape juice, of course.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: I think my children would prefer the castle to the vineyard! And the price?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That one's 55 pounds each.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And the third tour?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: That's the Coast Road. It's the longest, at 40 kilometres, and there are a few steep hills, so it's better for older children. Lunch used to be a picnic on the beach, but these days we stop at a seafood restaurant on the harbour. People say the food there is excellent.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: My husband won't eat the fish, of course.

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Don't worry, they have a very good vegetarian menu too.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: And what does the Coast Road cost?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: It was 58 pounds last year, but I'm afraid it's gone up. It's now 62 pounds per person.

script.speaker: helen
script.text: I see. Well, with the youngest only ten, I think the Valley Trail sounds best for us. Can I book that now?

script.speaker: oliver
script.text: Of course. I'll just need a few payment details.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A local food festival
parts.context: The director of a food festival is interviewed on local radio.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the director of a food festival talking on local radio. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Good morning, and welcome back to Weekend Live. With the Portmere Food Festival just two weeks away, I'm delighted to have the festival director, Rachel Moore, here in the studio. Welcome, Rachel.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Thanks for having me. It's lovely to be here.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: So, the festival has been going for twenty years now. How did it all start?

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Well, a lot of people assume it was set up to bring tourists to the town, and of course it does that very well now. But that wasn't the original idea. Twenty years ago, the fishing industry here was going through a really difficult time, and a group of local families decided to hold a small market on the seafront to sell their food and raise money for the fishing community. It grew from there.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: When the harbour was rebuilt, we moved everything down to the new quayside, and that's where it's been ever since.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: And what's new this year?

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Well, some people have asked us to make it a three-day event, and we did think about it, but in the end we decided to keep it to two days. And it's still on the quayside, of course. The big change is that, for the first time, entry is completely free. In the past it cost eight pounds for an adult, but this year a local company has agreed to cover our costs, so everyone can just walk in.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: That's great news. Now, the cookery demonstrations are always popular, aren't they?

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: They are. Last year we had to turn a lot of people away, which was a shame. So this year, if you'd like to watch a demonstration, you'll need to reserve a seat on our website before you come. It's free, but you do have to book. The demonstrations used to take place in the town hall, but this year they'll be in a big marquee next to the harbour, so there's more room. And for younger visitors, there's a separate children's kitchen, where they can make their own pizzas.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: Any advice for people planning to come?

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Yes, a couple of things. Parking in the town centre is very limited, so please don't try to drive into town. We're running a park and ride bus from the leisure centre every ten minutes, and that's by far the easiest way to get here.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: Also, we're trying to cut down on plastic this year, so please bring your own bags for anything you buy. People often ask whether they need to bring cash, but almost all the stallholders take cards now, so that isn't necessary. Unlike some festivals, you don't need to buy tokens before you can get food. You just pay the stallholders directly. And there's no need to arrive really early. It's busy all day, but Saturday afternoon is usually a bit quieter than the morning.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: So, what's happening on each day?

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: On Saturday morning, we open with the farmers' market, where you can buy fruit, vegetables and meat straight from local farms. That's on the Saturday only, because the farmers want to be back on their farms on Sunday.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: The cheese tasting was on Sunday last year, but this time we've moved it to Saturday, because it clashed with another event.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: There'll be live music all weekend, on both days, from midday until the festival closes.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: The chef's challenge, where local restaurants compete to cook the best fish dish, is always the last event of the festival, so that's on Sunday evening.

script.speaker: rachel
script.text: And finally, the bread-making workshops. We were only going to run them on Sunday, but so many people wanted places that we've added extra sessions on Saturday as well, so they'll be on both days.

script.speaker: presenter
script.text: It all sounds wonderful. Rachel Moore, thank you for joining us.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A project on citizen science
parts.context: Two students discuss their project with their tutor.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Maya and Josh, talking to their tutor about a project on citizen science. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: Come in, both of you. So, how's the citizen science project going?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Quite well, I think. We've been reading about lots of projects where members of the public help scientists to collect data.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: Did anything surprise you?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Yes, the national garden bird survey. I knew that huge numbers of people take part every year, but I had no idea it had been running for more than forty years. That's an amazing amount of data.

script.speaker: josh
script.text: I was more interested in whether the data is actually any good.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: And what did you conclude?

script.speaker: josh
script.text: Well, people often say that volunteers lose interest and give up, but the research suggests most of them stay involved for years. And the projects are cheap to run, compared with paying researchers. For me, the real weakness is that every volunteer records things differently. One person counts every single bird they see, and another just writes 'lots'. So it's hard to combine the results.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: That's a very good point. Now, looking at your plan, I'm a little worried. You've got notes on about ten different projects.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Is that too many?

script.speaker: evans
script.text: I think so. You've already done plenty of reading, so that isn't the issue. And I know you mentioned interviewing some volunteers, which would be nice, but I don't think there's time before the deadline. What I'd really suggest is choosing just one project and looking at it in depth.

script.speaker: josh
script.text: OK. So which one? The galaxy project is fascinating.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: It is, but it all happens online, so we wouldn't be able to see how the data is actually used. And the bird survey is far too big for us. What about the river-testing group? They test the water in the river right next to the campus.

script.speaker: josh
script.text: Oh, that's a good idea. We could even take part ourselves.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: I like that. The river project it is, then. So what's your first step?

script.speaker: josh
script.text: I suppose we could start writing a questionnaire for the volunteers.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: I think that can wait until we've met them. And we'll go down to the river on the next testing day anyway. Before anything else, we should email the organisers and ask if they're happy for us to join them.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: Yes, I'd certainly do that first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: Do you know how the river project actually works?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Yes, I read about it on their website. New volunteers don't need any experience. They just go to a training session, where they learn how to use the testing kit.

script.speaker: josh
script.text: Then, once a month, each volunteer goes to the same point on the river and collects samples of the water. It has to be the same spot every time, so that the results can be compared.

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Some volunteers also take photographs of the river bank, but that's optional.

script.speaker: josh
script.text: They test the water there and then, and they upload the results to the project's website, where anyone can see them.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: What happens if the results look strange?

script.speaker: maya
script.text: Then another sample is taken and sent to a laboratory at the university, to check whether there really is a problem, or whether the volunteer just made a mistake.

script.speaker: josh
script.text: And at the end of each year, the organisers send all the data to the local council. The council uses it to produce a map showing where the pollution problems are, so it knows which parts of the river to clean up first.

script.speaker: evans
script.text: Excellent. That gives you a clear structure for your report.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: seed banks
parts.context: A lecture about why seed banks matter and how they work.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about seed banks. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about seed banks: collections of seeds that are stored so that plants can be grown again in the future, even if they disappear from farms and from the wild.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Let's start with why they matter. A hundred years ago, farmers around the world grew many thousands of different varieties of crops. Today, most of our food comes from a much smaller number of high-yielding varieties. That's efficient, but it's also risky.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The old varieties that farmers have abandoned often carry genes that help plants resist disease. If a new disease attacks wheat, for example, the solution might be found in a variety that nobody has grown for fifty years. But only if someone has kept its seeds.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first person to collect seeds on a really large scale was the Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov, in the 1920s. He and his team travelled across five continents, and they built up a collection of hundreds of thousands of samples in the city that was then called Leningrad.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: During the Second World War, the city was surrounded for almost nine hundred days, and food ran out. The scientists guarding the collection were surrounded by rice, potatoes and grain, but they refused to eat any of it. Several of them died of hunger at their desks, because they believed the seeds were too important for the future.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So how are seeds stored today? When a seed bank receives a new sample, the seeds are cleaned, and then their moisture content is reduced until it is very low. This is essential, because if water remains inside a seed, it can form ice crystals when the seed is frozen, and these damage the cells.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The seeds are then sealed in foil packets, which keep out air and water, and they're stored at around minus eighteen degrees Celsius. Under these conditions, the seeds of many crops can survive for decades, and some for centuries.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The best-known seed bank is the Global Seed Vault on Svalbard, a group of Arctic islands that belong to Norway. It opened in 2008, and it's built deep inside a mountain, more than a hundred metres into the rock.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The location was chosen very carefully. The ground there is permanently frozen, so even if the electricity supply failed, the permafrost would keep the seeds below freezing.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The vault is sometimes compared to a safe-deposit box in a bank. Countries and research institutes send copies of their seeds, but they keep ownership of them, and only the depositor can take them out again.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For its first seven years, nothing was taken out. Then, in 2015, a research centre that had been based near Aleppo was forced to leave Syria because of the war. It asked for some of its seeds back, so that it could rebuild its collection in Lebanon and Morocco.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Seed banks do have limitations, though. Some plants produce seeds that simply cannot be stored in this way. The seeds of avocado, cocoa and oak trees, for example, die if they are dried, so they can't be frozen in the normal way.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For species like these, scientists use other methods. One is to take tiny pieces of plant tissue and freeze them very quickly in liquid nitrogen, at around minus one hundred and ninety-six degrees. Another is simply to grow the plants in living collections, such as botanic gardens.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Seed banks can't replace the protection of plants in the wild, but they are a vital insurance policy for the future of our food.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
